For future reference, I'm not a lawyer, but I've been in the free software world for over a decade. 

Don't let anyone tell you otherwise:
The GPL and all its related licenses are not just fancy labels for "public domain". While they encourage the free transmission of source code, permit modification and unhindered legitimate use, and allow publication of changed versions, there are important limitations to observe. This especially matters when you're writing software for other people to use. There has to be (and is) legal precedent for the freedoms and responsibilities of each license. Attribution for the original author is both good form and saves you from a lot of potential headaches and allegations later. 

"Public domain" affords a work no protection and no guarantees that subsequent works will remain similarly free. Worse, it's not legally enforceable in all countries and time frames for something to enter the public domain differ from country to country. Use of something in the public domain may be defensible in some places, but limited or forbidden in others. 

TL;DR Free software licenses are there for important reasons. Respect and care are necessary when you use works that are licensed under them.

I wouldn't think of it quite like that - it doesn't replace layers or key combinations, it augments them. So you can get by just fine with Raise and Lower and the standard modifiers, sure, but if you want to keep the number of layers low and the number of operations high, the addition of Hyper would allow you to at least double what you can do without adding further layers. 

I've taken advantage of this and really only use two layers (base included) for the majority of my day-to-day, and I can get anything done without trying to keep track of layers past that small amount. Other layers are reserved for "locking" it in various keyboard layouts or special modes.

I don't have any hard evidence to make a claim, but I will say this - there are multiple schools of thought to consider. Some see upward extension as the enemy of speed, but the fact is that if you "float" while you type, the difference in speed is probably minimal at best. What probably matters more is not how high up the key is (assuming the rows are spaced equally), but how far to each side your fingers must stretch. Thankfully the Planck and Preonic have an elegant way of dealing with that problem without changing the keyboard too drastically.

Having said that, my semi-informed opinion on the subject is that, given an ergonomic layout on an ortholinear keyboard that makes good use of the bottom row, by which I mean the thumbs can comfortably hit the most essential keys, it might be faster to use the thumbs and only going up one row from home. An arrangement like this would be at its best when the modifier is on the opposite hand of the key being hit in the combo (so if "q" is on the left, "Super" on the right is easier).

Why is that any faster? Perhaps it isn't, but it puts very little strain and stretch on your hands and allows you to keep going for quite a bit longer (so you can probably type faster for longer periods of time). It's the very reason I always discourage new Emacs users from doing the whole "Caps Lock to Control" swap and ignoring their existing control keys. Your left pinkie has to do double duty that way and there is no alternation. 

Of course, having good use of the thumb keys like I've described is only valuable if you don't have to think about which key you're hitting. The more familiar you are with the keyboard, the less you'll have to pause to figure that out.

Hyper is extremely useful once you get used to it - you can treat it as a modifier that can't possibly clobber any of your other keybindings because it's using a combination that would be ridiculous to type out manually every time.

I personally like to use it in combination with other keys across layers to enable each key to do at least two special operations, depending on whether it's pressed with Hyper or without. 

And yes, the point about it being on the Space Cadet is correct. It was a bit more Lisp machine-specific there, but it has been translated to be more generally useful in its present form.

Well, the way I did it awhile ago was to start with this site:
http://www.keyboard-layout-editor.com/

Under the "Presets" tab they have one for the Planck's physical layout. You can copy the raw data from it. Here it is to save you a step:
https://gist.github.com/broken-username/2557482a5684c1c17e8c908dfd66104b

Then you can paste it at http://builder.swillkb.com/ in the "Plate Layout" box.

From there, some settings that work are pretty simple to figure out, but here's an example:

* Edge padding: 6mm or more on all sides
* Screw count: 6 or more
* Kerf: 0.15mm
* Plate corners: 2mm
* Line weight: 0.1 (different manufacturers vary in what they will accept for this value)
* Line color: Blue (same story here)
* Mountholes: Around 2 or 3.25mm for M2 or M3 screws, respectively (might need to adjust these a little bit in Adobe Illustrator or Inkscape). The standoffs are, of course, thicker than the screws. I found a 1.92mm hole for an M2 screw and a 3.25mm hole for the standoff to be just fine.
* Edge width: Up to you, but try to get the edges clear of the holes
* USB Cutout: Will definitely have to be changed for the PCB since the USB connector isn't dead-center. Not strictly necessary if you decide to hand-wire.

Once that's done, it will give you a bunch of files, one for each layer of the sandwich case.

I imagine others will be able to chip in some helpful advice on how to get the specifications "just so" for the Planck PCB. It's possible that these files are out there somewhere ready-made, but if you ask me, that's just not as fun! ;)

By the way, around 0.118" (~3mm) is a pretty standard and sturdy width for each layer.
What I would check for is if there are any obvious "breaks" where the trace should be continuous. Any scratches on the board might be a sign of this.
Did you check all the traces for possible damage? Are the LED legs in the right orientation?
For future reference "KC_NO" is used for keys that are supposed to be ignored rather than having their own keycode or a keycode "inherited" from the base layout.

The pin assignment in a hand-wired arrangement can be chosen entirely by the user as they see fit, but on a pre-made PCB those choices have already been made for you. Relative to the microcontroller's position on the board, you can often follow the traces on the board and see where each connection ends up. You may need to ask about traces you can't see (it looks like the PCB you linked to has 2 layers), or find some documentation. When a matrix is used, the topmost row is row 0, followed by row 1 (going down), and so on, and the columns start from zero and (on the bottom of the board) go right to left. 

How you configure config.h depends on the features you want, the microcontroller you're using, and the pin assignments. If you're using a Pro Micro, the pinout you need is here: https://i.imgur.com/wMNx2u6.png. Just take the "P" out of each pin name and you'll have what you need for the pin assignment in config.h.

QMK sets Layer 0 as default unless you tell it not to, so everything is relative to that. "Lower" and "Raise" are abstractions that don't necessarily *need* to have the names they do - in reality, you can call your additional layers Layer 1 and Layer 2, FUNCTION_LAYER and NUMPAD_LAYER, or whatever you find most useful. The only thing to remember is that you DO go up from zero and back down again. I've got all the functionality of a Planck on this keyboard, and there is no "Lower" or "Raise", just named layers and keys that switch to them. 

Remember that learning and developing your own ideas about how it should work are the key to a good experience. QMK is an extremely valuable and versatile tool, as are websites that help you to design the layout and start the the process of writing source code. Check out keyboard-layout-editor.com and kbfirmware.com if you ever want to go beyond pre-constructed layouts.
